# Where AI might plug in

## What even is AI?

- Machine learning (i.e. statistics)
- Neural networks (i.e. statistics)
- Physics informed neural networks (i.e. statistics and mathematical
  modelling)
- Universal differential equations (i.e. statistics and mathematical
  modelling)
- Reinforcement learning
- Attention based neural networks
- Large language models
- My friendly agentic CLI tool (i.e. claude code)

## My view {.center}

::: {style="font-size: 1.25em; margin-top: 0.6em;"}
Many of these approaches are under-explored and not well integrated with
the rapidly evolving, noisy, sparse data settings I have worked in.
I am not aware of any real-world operational use so far, and I am mostly
not convinced by the evaluations of proposed methods.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em; margin-top: 1em; color: #4a5899;"}
Sam Abbott, September 2026
:::

## And yet {.center}

::: {style="font-size: 1.6em; margin-top: 0.8em;"}
I am very excited about their potential.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em; margin-top: 1em; color: #4a5899;"}
Sam Abbott, September 2026
:::

## Universal differential equations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- A universal differential equation (UDE) is a differential equation
  with one or more terms a neural network, fitted jointly with the
  mechanistic parameters. Rackauckas et al. 2020
- Applied to epidemics by Dandekar, Rackauckas and Barbastathis 2020. A
  network for quarantine strength in a susceptible, infectious,
  recovered model, fitted to case counts from 70 countries
- Reporting is not modelled, and there is no comparison with a simple
  semi-mechanistic model. Philipps et al. 2025 found that noise and
  limited data degrade the fit and the mechanistic parameters lose
  their meaning
- Charlotte Holt, epiforecasts PhD student, is using UDEs to try and
  recover behavioural change in outbreaks and improve forecasts
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/exchange-seir-vs-ude.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Left, a semi-mechanistic stochastic SEIR box model with the
transmission rate a random walk and one arrow to a cases box, labelled
the rate is free to move and one stream constrains it. Right, the same
SEIR boxes with the transmission rate a neural network fed by mobility,
surveys, policy, weather and wastewater, and an arrow to cases, deaths
and admissions, labelled the rate is learned from many sources."}

::: {.attribution}
Dandekar, Rackauckas and Barbastathis 2020, Patterns,
[doi:10.1016/j.patter.2020.100145](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2020.100145)
· Philipps, Schmid and Hasenauer 2025, npj Syst Biol Appl,
[PMC12398592](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12398592/)
:::
:::
::::

## A neural network in the slots of a composable model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- **A network in the $R_t$ slot.** It learns what the autoregressive
  (AR) process cannot say. Behaviour, season, policy
- **A network on the observation side.** Several data streams fitted
  from the same latent infections
- Most exciting where there are many hard to model data sets to fit
  jointly in an otherwise well understood system
- No neural network code in any EpiAware package yet
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/exchange-nn-component.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Three boxes in a row: an infection model, Renewal with an
empty rt slot, an observation model of LatentDelay, Ascertainment and
NegativeBinomialError, and cases. Two candidates point at the R_t slot:
an AR process, labelled today, and a small neural network of
covariates, labelled a question, with a swap arrow between them. Under
the observation model a third candidate, a network from the latent
infections to cases, deaths and wastewater at once."}
:::
::::

## Physics-informed neural networks

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- A physics-informed neural network (PINN) maps time to the model
  state, $S(t)$, $I(t)$, $R(t)$. The loss adds the residual of the
  differential equation to the misfit with the data
- Time-varying parameters such as the transmission rate $\beta_t$ come
  out of the same fit. Kharazmi et al. 2021 on New York City, Rhode
  Island, Michigan and Italy
- The equation constrains the fit where surveillance series are short
  or noisy. Millevoi et al. 2024 fitted Italian COVID-19 cases and
  admissions jointly, and found extrapolation past the training window
  can go far from the data
- Deterministic, so no uncertainty quantification by default
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/exchange-pinn.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="A schematic. A time input feeds a neural network. The network
outputs the model state S, I and R and the transmission rate. The state
goes to a data loss, the misfit to reported cases; the state and the
rate go to a physics loss, the residual of the differential equations,
with automatic differentiation supplying the derivatives. The two losses
sum to one training loss."}

::: {.attribution}
Raissi, Perdikaris and Karniadakis 2019, J Comput Phys,
[doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045)
· Millevoi, Pasetto and Ferronato 2024, PLOS Comput Biol,
[doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012387](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012387)
:::
:::
::::

## Renewal processes as a neural network layer

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- A specialised form of PINN
- A renewal process is an autoregressive transformation of $R_t$ and
  past infections to today's infections. It can be thought of as a
  neural network layer
- Stacked with other layers. Inputs to $R_t$, an $R_t$ layer,
  observation layers, and multiple data streams
- Against a PINN on a differential equation, time-varying parameters
  are natural to a renewal process, and its discrete time matches the
  data
- Not seen this used in research yet. Proposed in Samuel Brand's
  `RenewalExamples` repository

::: {.attribution}
Samuel Brand, [github.com/SamuelBrand1/RenewalExamples][rex] · Pervez,
Locatello and Gavves 2024, *Mechanistic Neural Networks*
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/exchange-renewal-layer.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="On the left the renewal equation, I_t equals R_t times the sum
over s of I_{t minus s} g_s, described as a convolution with a fixed
kernel scaled by R_t. On the right a stack of six layers: inputs, an R_t
layer marked learned, then a renewal layer, a delay layer and an
ascertainment layer marked fixed by the epidemiology, then a negative
binomial likelihood on each stream."}
:::
::::

## An outbreak-specific foundation model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- **Time series foundation models.** Pretrained on many series from
  other domains. Your series in, a forecast out, no fitting
- Good a few weeks out on sparse data. Less good at peaks and turning
  points
- **CAPE** pretrains on simulated compartmental epidemics. A model of
  outbreaks, but of the final curves
- **Outbreak data change after the fact.** On the DRC model the daily
  suspected stream stopped on 6 August. In May INSP, the DRC's public
  health institute, reclassified suspected cases
- How do these methods hold up when the data change under them, in
  prospective settings?

::: {.attribution}
Kalahasti et al. 2025, medRxiv,
[doi:10.1101/2025.02.24.25322795](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.24.25322795v1)
· Liu et al. 2026, CAPE, KDD
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/exchange-foundation-outbreak.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Left, the same outbreak curve as it looked in May, July and
September, each vintage lower and shorter than the next, with a dashed
line where the case definition changed, and below it bars showing data
streams that start and stop. Middle, an arrow labelled every vintage,
every stream, with its date, into a box labelled an outbreak foundation
model pretrained on outbreaks as they were seen at the time. Right, a
nowcast and forecast fan on the latest vintage."}

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 0.3em; color: #4a5899;"}
